analysis.title: Rethinking the 60/40 portfolio: what can bitcoin provide?
key_insights: Higher inflation and interest rates are keeping stock-bond correlations positive, weakening a core assumption of the traditional 60/40 portfolio.
Through the 2000s and 2010s, weak growth, low inflation and near-zero rates meant equity weakness coincided with falling yields. That negative correlation underpinned 60/40.
Post-pandemic inflation forced a sharp rate reset that hit both bond prices and equity valuations. Bonds still provide income but may not diversify enough on their own.
Fidelity outlines a 60/20/20 framework in which equities stay the anchor, bonds keep the income role, and part of the bond sleeve goes to assets with low or negative correlation to stocks and bonds.

Bitcoin combines gold-like scarcity from limited supply with technology network growth viewed through Metcalfe's law. It may act as a store of value in some environments and a higher-growth risk asset in others.
Bitcoin may sit alongside gold in the diversifying sleeve, so an allocation could be funded from the 40% bond allocation rather than the 60% equity allocation.
Neither bitcoin nor gold generates cash flows, so DCF does not apply. One alternative is comparing price with its long-term power-law curve and historical support trend.

During the 2026 Iran conflict, central-bank demand and speculative flows pushed gold well above its longer-term trend while bitcoin stayed subdued. Under the model presented, bitcoin looked undervalued relative to gold.
A key test of maturation is whether bitcoin behaves like an established store of value. The slope of its rallies and the size of its declines have moderated over successive cycles.
The report carries a risk warning that digital assets are speculative, highly volatile, can become illiquid, and investors could lose their entire investment.
crypto_views: Bitcoin pairs gold-like scarcity with technology network growth and could be considered alongside gold as a diversifier funded from the bond allocation.
Moderating rally slopes and drawdown magnitudes across cycles may signal bitcoin's gradual maturation as an asset class.

Valuation can use the power-law curve and historical support trend, plus a relative view against gold. Under the model presented, bitcoin looked undervalued versus gold after the 2026 Iran conflict gold run.
Digital assets are speculative and highly volatile, and investors could lose the entire value of their investment.
risk_factors: Positive stock-bond correlation under higher inflation and rates undermines 60/40 diversification.
Bitcoin may behave as a higher-growth risk asset rather than a store of value in some environments.
Bitcoin has no cash flows, so valuation relies on model-based frameworks such as the power-law curve.
Digital assets can become illiquid at any time and carry total loss risk.
vol_and_positioning: Bitcoin's declines and rallies have moderated over successive cycles, which Fidelity reads as a possible shift away from its boom and bust profile.
geopolitical: The 2026 Iran conflict drove central-bank demand and speculative flows into gold, pushing it well above its longer-term trend.

tension_points.bull_case: Bitcoin combines gold-like scarcity with network growth, and its moderating cycle swings could support a more established allocation role funded from bonds.
tension_points.bear_case: Bitcoin may behave like a higher-growth risk asset in some environments, and it has no cash flows to anchor valuation.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Bitcoin failing to moderate its rally slopes and drawdowns over successive cycles, which would show it has not matured into a reliable store of value.

theme_stances.key_argument: Bonds diversify less with positive stock-bond correlation, so bitcoin may join gold in a diversifying sleeve funded from the bond allocation.
theme_stances.evidence: an allocation could therefore come from the traditional 40% bond allocation
